en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on the Determination of Formless Phenomena: 3.
The Question on the Effort to Abandon Suffering
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, do you strive for the abandoning of past suffering?
"No, Great King," he replied.
“But, venerable sir, do you strive for the abandoning of future suffering?
“No, great king.
“Then do you strive for the abandoning of present suffering?”
“Indeed not, Great King.
“If you do not strive for the abandoning of past suffering, nor strive for the abandoning of future suffering, nor strive for the abandoning of present suffering, then for what purpose do you strive?
The Elder replied:
“It is for this purpose, Great King, that we strive: ‘How might this suffering cease, and no other suffering arise?
“But, venerable Nāgasena, do you have future suffering?
“There is none, Great King.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, you are indeed exceedingly wise, since you strive for the abandoning of sufferings that are non-existent and have not yet come to pass.
“But, Great King, do you have any rival kings, adversaries, or enemies standing against you?
“Yes, venerable sir, there are.”
“Great King, would you then have had a moat dug, a rampart built, a gate-tower constructed, a watchtower erected, and grain brought in?
“No, venerable sir; that was prepared beforehand.
“Great King, would you then have trained in elephants, trained in horses, trained in chariots, trained in the bow, or trained in the sword?”
“Indeed not, venerable sir; it was trained for that only after the fact.
“For what purpose?
“Venerable sir, for the purpose of warding off dangers yet to come.”
“Great King, is there indeed such a thing as future danger?
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Great King, you are truly very wise, you who prepare yourselves to ward off dangers that do not yet exist and have not yet come to pass.”
“Give me another simile,” he said.
“What do you think, great king? When you are thirsty, would you then have a well dug, or a lotus pond excavated, or a reservoir constructed, thinking, ‘I shall drink water’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir; that has already been prepared beforehand.”
“For what purpose?
“It is prepared, venerable sir, for the purpose of warding off future thirsts.
“But, great king, does future thirst exist?”
“There is not, venerable sir.
“Then you, Great King, are exceedingly wise, you who prepare that [water] for the purpose of warding off thirsts that do not yet exist and have not yet come.
“Give me a further simile,” he said.
“What do you think, great king? When you are hungry, would you then have a field plowed and rice sown, thinking, ‘I shall eat a meal’?
“No, venerable sir; that has already been prepared beforehand.
“For what purpose?”
“It is for the purpose of warding off future hunger, venerable sir.
“But, great king, does future hunger exist?
“No, venerable sir.”
“You are indeed very wise, Great King, you who prepare [this food] for the purpose of warding off the hunger of those who do not yet exist and have not yet come.
“You are clever, venerable Nāgasena.
The third question, concerning the exertion to abandon suffering, is finished.
